entries.name: The Society of Jesus, 1650 to 1814
entries.informalName: The Society of Jesus from 1650 to the restoration
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey as a Tier 1 entry for the window 1650 to 1814. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Good for the order's two ends and thin for the years between. The Library holds the pope's brief of suppression (1773) and his bull of restoration (1814). For the Paraguay towns it holds one book, by the librarian of the Duke of Modena, printed at Venice in 1743. Almost every text read is a Roman act or an outsider's account. entries.teaser: The Society of Jesus, 1650 to 1814. Its Paraguay towns. Its expulsion by four kings. Its suppression in 1773. Its former members in Russia, and the restoration.
entries.longDescription:
After 1650 the Society of Jesus carried on the order told in the earlier entry on the Society. Two acts of Rome frame these years. Clement XIV closed the Society by his brief of 21 July 1773. Pius VII restored it by his bull of 7 August 1814.

In Paraguay the Jesuits ran towns for the Guaraní people. Such towns were called reductions. In 1743 a book about them was printed at Venice. Its author, Muratori, was the Duke of Modena's librarian.

The name Reduction, he says, meant a people gathered and brought to live as a society and a commonwealth (a plain rendering). His title calls the work Happy Christianity.

In 1717, he says, there were more than thirty reductions. They held 121,178 souls. Jesuit fathers had baptized them all. They were the only missionaries. He also says that raiders from the Portuguese colony of São Paulo had once destroyed fourteen Christian reductions in the Guaraní country.

In 1741 Pope Benedict XIV wrote to the bishops of Brazil, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata. He condemned those who forced Indians into slavery or sold them, even baptized Indians. The bull does not name the Society.

Then the Catholic kings turned on the order. Clement XIV's brief says the kings of France, Spain, Portugal and Sicily felt forced to drive its members from their lands. Among its charges are quarrels over missions in Europe, Africa and America. It also names "certain idolatrous ceremonies adopted in certain places". The brief does not name China. The pope then suppressed the company. The entry on the Catholic Church of the old regime tells that act from Rome's side. In 1703 a Jesuit, François Noël, wrote from Rome, where he had been sent over the honors paid in China to Confucius and to the dead. The entry on the Catholic Church in China tells the Rites dispute and the court mission at Peking.

In Russia some of its former members carried on. Pius VII's bull says that Francis Kareu and other secular priests had lived many years in the empire. They had been members of the Company of Jesus. They asked leave to unite in a body. Emperor Paul I had recommended them in a dispatch of 11 August 1800. By a brief of 7 March 1801 the pope let them form a congregation of the Company in Russia, and he named Kareu its general. In 1804 he gave the same leave to the Two Sicilies. On 7 August 1814 he extended it to all states.

The Jesuits also worked in Transylvania. A synod text of 1701, printed by Nilles in 1886, says the talks of union with Rome began by the work and skill of the Jesuit fathers at Alba Iulia (in a plain English rendering). The entry on the Romanian Greek Catholic Church tells that union, which was signed in 1698.

This entry ends with the restoration. The Society's nineteenth-century story is not yet told in an entry of its own.

entries.name: Catholics of the Ottoman Balkans: the Bosnian Franciscans
entries.informalName: The Franciscan church of Bosnia and Slavonia
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey as a Tier 2 entry for the window 1650 to 1815. The later years, to 1878, wait for one more source. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Thin, and from one side. The Library holds a calendar of documents on Bosnia, in Latin, printed at Zagreb in 1892 and running to 1752. It prints Roman and Franciscan documents, among them a declaration in the name of the clergy and people, and not the people's own voice. No Franciscan chronicle in Croatian has been read. Nothing has been read on the Albanian or Bulgarian Catholics for these years.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry tells the Catholics of Bosnia and Slavonia from 1650 to 1815, served by the friars of the Bosnian province. The calendar that tells it is a Roman and Franciscan record. Its later years, to 1878, wait for one more source.
entries.why: The friars of the Bosnian province spoke for the clergy and the people of their parishes. In 1689 they declared at Požega that for at least 170 years no bishop but the bishop of Bosnia had ruled that church. In 1746 their provincial gathered proofs for the court at Vienna, to defend the province's own parishes in Slavonia.
entries.teaser: Bosnia and Slavonia, 1650 to 1815. The friars of the Bosnian province, and their fights over who held the Catholic parishes between the Sava and the Drava.
entries.longDescription:
The Catholics of Bosnia and the lands north of it were served by the friars of the Bosnian province. A calendar of their documents, in Latin, was printed at Zagreb in 1892. It is the main source for these years.

On 1 January 1689 the fathers of the Bosnian province met at Požega, in Slavonia. The calendar says they spoke in their own name and the people's. They declared that the bishops of Zagreb had never held jurisdiction in the Slavonian parts. The clergy and the Catholic people between the Sava and the Drava said that no bishop but the bishop of Bosnia had built up and ruled the church of Požega, for at least 170 years.

The Crown took a hand. In 1690, from Vienna, King Leopold ordered that the bishop of Bosnia be kept and defended in his rights in the district of Požega. This was to last until a judge had settled the questions.

In 1746 Franjo Ivanović wrote from Vienna to the guardians of Slavonia. He was provincial of Bosnia Argentina. That means Silver Bosnia (a plain rendering). He asked them to gather testimonies from nobles and faithful. The province would use them at the court of Vienna. They were to defend its rights in the Slavonian parishes.

These are records of fights about parishes. They show the friars speaking for their people. They do not show how the people themselves saw the friars.
voices: The fathers of the Bosnian province — who met at Požega on 1 January 1689 and spoke for the clergy and the people
Franjo Ivanović — provincial of Bosnia Argentina, who in 1746 asked the guardians of Slavonia for testimonies to defend the province's parishes
entries.legacy: In 1746 the province was still defending its parishes in Slavonia. The Library's calendar stops at 1752, so it does not show how that dispute ended. The years after 1815 wait for one more source.
entries.peopleNote: The calendar prints the 1689 declaration in Latin, in the name of the clergy and people. It also prints the opening lines of Ivanović's 1746 letter in Croatian, but the scan is too damaged to quote. No single friar's own words are quoted.

livingEvidence.basis: The Catholic Church of Bosnia and Croatia is alive today. This entry's sources end in 1815 and give no present-day evidence. No dated item after 2010 has been found for the friars' church of these years.

set.longDescription:
This was the Catholic Church at the height of its establishment and on the edge of its worst crisis: enormously wealthy, woven into the monarchies of Europe, and increasingly unable to control them. Rome's condemnation of Jansenism in the bull Unigenitus (1713) turned into a fifty-year political crisis in France, with parlements and bishops fighting over it. Then the Catholic monarchies turned on the church's most effective order, expelling the Jesuits from Portugal, France, Spain and Naples and forcing the pope to suppress the Society altogether in 1773. Then came the Revolution: church property nationalized, clergy required to swear to a Civil Constitution that split them into jurors and refractories, thousands killed or driven abroad, and Pope Pius VI carried off to die a French prisoner in 1799. His successor signed a concordat with Napoleon in 1801, was imprisoned by him in turn, outlived him, and restored the Jesuits in 1814.

Rome ran its missions through Propaganda, the congregation for spreading the faith. Its collected decrees show three acts in these years.

In 1656 the Holy Office ruled on a set of questions. Missionaries in China had sent them to Propaganda in 1645. Chinese Christians could keep certain rites, it said. The cult, it said, seemed merely civil and political.

In 1659 Propaganda sent orders to its vicars apostolic. They were not to urge any people to change its rites, customs and ways. What is more absurd, it asked, than to carry France, Spain or Italy into China (in a plain English rendering)?

In 1726 Propaganda ruled that native priests must swear an oath too. This covered China, Tonkin and Cochinchina. The oath was the one set by the constitution Ex illa die.

Between the fall of Napoleon and the eve of the First World War, the Catholic Church lost a state and gained a papacy. Gregory XVI and then Pius IX met the liberal century head-on: Pius defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854, cataloged the errors of the age in the Syllabus of 1864, and in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility. Weeks before Italian troops entered Rome and ended the Papal States. Stripped of territory, the papacy grew in reach instead: bishops and ordinary Catholics looked to Rome as never before, new congregations of sisters and brothers staffed schools and hospitals across the world, and mass devotion gathered around Marian apparitions like Lourdes in 1858. Under Leo XIII the church that had spent decades condemning the modern world began to negotiate with it, most consequentially in Rerum Novarum (1891), which put the church on the side of a worker's right to a living wage and to organize.

Rome still ran the missions through Propaganda. In 1845 it wrote to a vicar apostolic. It called it a grave abuse, not to be borne, to baptize again all whom catechists had baptized (a plain rendering).
